title: History and Related Topics
text:
The Inferential Model idea was originally inspired by ideas from Dempster-Shafer calculus (itself inspired by Fiducial inference). In the Dempster Shafer framework, they create Belief functions – an alternative way of describing evidence as opposed to probability. It was through the theory of Random Sets that the original IM solution came to be.
Later realizing that assuming monotonicity in Random Sets (the evidence concentrates at the MLE) corresponds directly to possibility theory, the corresponding implementation has become much cleaner.

title: Normal Distribution
text:
This page shows a toy example of how to construct a possibilistic inferential model (IM) when the data is assumed to come from a Normal distribution with mean \(\theta\) and variance \(1\).


To construct an inferential model, we first construct the relative likelihood: \[ R(x, \theta) = \frac{p_{\theta}(x)}{\sup_{\vartheta} p_\vartheta(x)}, \] where \(p_{\theta}(x)\) is the likelihood function with parameter \(\theta\) and observed data \(x\).
Assuming we observe \(x \in X\) and \(X \sim N(\theta, 1)\), the maximum likelihood estimator is \(\widehat{\theta}=x\).
\[\begin{align}
R(x,\theta) &= \frac{p_{\theta}(x)}{p_{\widehat{\theta}}(x)} = p_{\theta}(x) = p(|x-\theta|),
\end{align}\] where \(p\) is the density function for standard Normal distribution.



The next step is a validation step:
\[\pi_x(\theta) = P_\theta(R(X, \theta) \le R(x, \theta)).\]
For the Normal distribution, there is a closed form for the contour.
\[\begin{align}
\pi_x(\theta) &= P_\theta \{ p(X-\theta) \le p(x-\theta) \} \\
&= P_\theta \{ |X-\theta| \le |x-\theta|\} \\
&= 2 \{1 - P(|x-\theta|) \},
\end{align}\] where \(P\) is the cumulative distribution function for standard Normal distribution. The above derivation works for sample size \(n=1\). When \(n>1\), the sample mean (\(\bar{x}\)) and the sample variance (\(1/\sqrt{n}\)) are used instead.
\[\pi_x(\theta) = 2 \{ 1 - P(\sqrt{n} \cdot |\bar{x} - \theta| ) \}.\]
The code below finds the contour function \(\pi_x(\theta)\) given observation \(x\) and the parameter of interest \(\theta\).

contour_normal <- function(x, theta){
  x_bar <- mean(x)
  n <- length(x)
  return(2 * (pnorm(abs(x_bar-theta)*sqrt(n), lower.tail = F) ))
}




Now we assume the true parameter is \(0\) and sample size is \(1\), let’s plot the contour function given that we observed \(x=1\).

n <- 1
true_theta <- 0
X <- 1

theta <- seq(true_theta-6, true_theta+6, .1)
pi_normal <- contour_normal(X, theta)
plot(theta, pi_normal, type = "l", xlab = expression(theta), ylab = expression(pi[x](theta)))
pi_true_theta <- contour_normal(X, true_theta)
abline(h=.05, lty=2)
segments(-1, 0, 0, 0, col="red", lwd=2)
segments(0, 0, 0, contour_normal(X,0), lty=3, col="red")
points(0, contour_normal(X,0), col="red", pch=19)








As shown above, the black curve is the contour function for \(x=1\). The possibility measure (or upper probability) of the hypothesis \(h=[-1,0]\) can be found by maximization:
\[ \Pi_x(h) = \sup_{\theta \in [-1,0]} \pi_x(\theta) \approx 0.317,\] where the red circle is.
To find a \(95\%\) confidence set, the black dashed line at \(0.05\) shows that the set is approximately \([-1, 3]\).

title: Random Effect Model
text:
This page shows a toy example of how to construct a possibilistic inferential model (IM) for a random effect model.
\[\begin{align*}
    X_{ij} &= Z_i+\epsilon_{ij},
    \\     
    X_{ij} &| Z_i \sim N(Z_i, \sigma^2_\epsilon), \\
    Z_i & \sim N(0, \sigma^2_Z).
\end{align*}\] for \(i = 1, \cdots, m\) and \(j = 1, \cdots, n\).
For example, if we set \(m=5, n=3\), here is one example of the data.

m <- 5 
n <- 3
sig2 <- 7
tau2 <- 5
x <- sqrt(sig2) * matrix(rnorm(m * n), nrow=m) + sqrt(tau2) * rnorm(m)
boxplot(c(x[1,]), c(x[2,]), c(x[3,]), c(x[4,]), c(x[5,]))










To construct an inferential model, we first construct the relative likelihood: \[ R(x, \theta) = \frac{p_{\theta}(x)}{\sup_{\vartheta} p_\vartheta(x)} = \exp \left( \log p_\theta(x) - \log p_{\hat{\theta}}(x) \right),\] where \(p_{\theta}(x)\) is the likelihood function. The marginal log likelihood is \[\begin{align*}
\log P(X) &=
-\frac{mn}{2} \log(2 \pi) - \frac{m(n-1)}{2} \log(\sigma^2_\epsilon) \\
& - \frac{m}{2} \log(\sigma^2_\epsilon + n \sigma^2_Z) - \frac{\sum_i \sum_j (x_{ij} - \bar{x_{i\cdot}})^2}{2\sigma^2_\epsilon} - \frac{n \sum_i \bar{x_{i\cdot}^2}}{2(\sigma^2_\epsilon + n\sigma^2_Z)}.
\end{align*}\] The maximum likelihood estimators are: \[\begin{align*}
    \hat{\sigma}^2_\epsilon &= \frac{\sum_i \sum_j (x_{ij} - \bar{x}_i)^2}{m(n-1)}, \\
    \hat{\sigma}^2_Z &= \frac{1}{n} \left( \frac{n \sum_i \bar{x}_i^2}{m} - \frac{\sum_i \sum_j (x_{ij} - \bar{x}_i)^2 }{m(n-1)} \right),
\end{align*}\] where \(\bar{x}_i = \frac{1}{n} \sum_j x_{ij}\). Now we have all the pieces to calculate the relative likelihood.



The next step is a validation step:
\[\pi_x(\theta) = P_\theta(R(X, \theta) \le R(x, \theta)).\]
The code below finds the contour function \(\pi_x(\theta)\) given observation \(x\) and the parameter of interest \(\theta\).

get.suff.stat <- function(x) {
  
  xbar.i <- rowMeans(x)
  xbar <- mean(x)
  out <- c(sum((x - xbar.i)**2), sum((xbar.i)**2))
  return(out)
  
}

# marginal loglikelihood without the latent variable
logrellik <- function(x, sig2, tau2){
  m <- nrow(x)
  n <- ncol(x)
  S <- get.suff.stat(x)
  sig2_hat <- S[1]/(m*(n-1))
  tau2_hat <- (n*S[2]/m - S[1]/(m*(n-1)))/n
  
  f <- function(u) {
    
    s2 <- exp(u[1])
    t2 <- exp(u[2])
    o1 <- m * (n - 1) * log(s2) + m * log(s2 + n * t2)
    o2 <- S[1] / s2 + n * S[2] / (s2 + n * t2)
    return( -(o1 + o2) / 2 )
    
  }
  
  out <- list( logrellik = f(c(sig2, tau2)) - f(c(sig2_hat, tau2_hat)))
  return(out)
} 




Now assume we observe data from \(m=30\) groups and each grup has \(n=5\) repeated measures. Let’s plot the contour function.

m <- 30
n <- 5
sig2 <- .5 
tau2 <- .6
size <- 100

thetaZ <- seq(.1, 1.7, by=.02)
thetaE <- seq(.1, .9, by=.02)
pi <- outer(thetaZ, thetaE)

e <- sqrt(sig2) * matrix(rnorm(m * n), nrow=m) 
z <- sqrt(tau2) * rnorm(m)
x <- e+z

for (i in seq_along(thetaZ)){
  for (j in seq_along(thetaE)){
    
    ttau2 <- thetaZ[i]^2
    ssig2 <- thetaE[j]^2
    
    LHS <- rep(NA, size)
    
    for (s in 1:size){
      
      Z <- sqrt(ttau2) * rnorm(m)
      E <- sqrt(ssig2) * matrix(rnorm(m * n), nrow = m)
      X <- E + Z
      
      LHS[s] <- logrellik(X, ssig2, ttau2)$logrellik
      
    }
    RHS <- logrellik(x, ssig2, ttau2)$logrellik
    pi[i, j] <- mean(LHS <= RHS)
    
  }
}

plot(0, 0, type = "n", xlim = c(.1, 1.7), ylim = c(.1, .9), xlab = expression(sigma[Z]), ylab = expression(sigma[E]), main=paste0("m=",m,", n=",n))
contour(thetaZ, thetaE, pi, drawlabels=TRUE, add=TRUE)
contour(thetaZ, thetaE, pi, levels=c(.1,1),add=TRUE, col="magenta")
points(sqrt(tau2), sqrt(sig2), col="red", pch=19)








As shown above, the contour plot is now two-dimensional. The red dot is where the true variances are, and the two magenta curves mark the \(90\%\) confidence region.

title: Binomial
text:
This page shows a toy example of how to construct a possibilistic inferential model (IM) when the data is assumed to come from a Binomial distribution with \(n\) trials and probability of success \(\theta\).


To construct an inferential model, we first construct the relative likelihood: \[ R(x, \theta) = \frac{p_{\theta}(x)}{\sup_{\vartheta} p_\vartheta(x)}, \] where \(p_{\theta}(x)\) is the likelihood function of Bin(\(n, \theta\)):
\[p_\theta(x) = \begin{pmatrix} n \\ x \end{pmatrix} \theta^x (1-\theta)^{n-x}, \quad x = 0, 1, \cdots, n, \quad \theta \in [0, 1].\] The maximum likelihood estimator of a Binomial distribution is \(\frac{x}{n}\). Thus the relative likelihood is:
\[R(x, \theta) = \frac{p_\theta(x)}{p_{\widehat{\theta}}(x)} = \left( \frac{n\theta}{x}\right)^x \left( \frac{n - n\theta}{n-x}\right)^{n-x} \]



The next step is a validation step:
\[\pi_x(\theta) = P_\theta(R(X, \theta) \le R(x, \theta)).\]
For the Binomial distribution, there is a closed form for the contour.
\[\pi_x(\theta) = \sum_{y=0}^n 1 \{ R(y, \theta) \le R(x, \theta) \} p_\theta(y).\]
The code below finds the contour function \(\pi_x(\theta)\) given observation \(x\) and the parameter of interest \(\theta\).

R_binomial <- function(x, n, theta){
  
  R <- (n*theta/x)^x * (n*(1-theta)/(n-x))^(n-x)
  return(R)
  
}

# closed form for x=n
contour_binomial <- function(theta, n, x){
  
  RHS <- R_binomial(x, n, theta)
  total <- 0
  for (i in 0:n){
    total <- total + (1*(R_binomial(i, n, theta) <= RHS)) * dbinom(i, n, theta)
  }
  return(total)
  
}




Now assume we observe \(6\) successes from \(10\) trilas, let’s plot the contour function.

n <- 10
x <- 6

theta <- seq(0.01, .99, by = .005)

pi_binomial <- contour_binomial(theta, n, x)
plot(theta, pi_binomial, type = "l", xlab = expression(theta), ylab = expression(pi[x](theta)))
abline(h=.05, lty=2)
segments(0.3, 0, 0.5, 0, col="red", lwd=2)
segments(0.5, 0, 0.5, contour_binomial(0.5, n, x), lty=3, col="red")
points(0.5, contour_binomial(0.5, n, x), col="red", pch=19)








As shown above, the black curve is the contour function for \(x=6\). The possibility measure (or upper probability) of the hypothesis \(h=[0.3,0.5]\) can be found by maximization:
\[ \Pi_x(h) = \sup_{\theta \in [0.3,0.5]} \pi_x(\theta) \approx 0.754,\] where the red circle is.
To find a \(95\%\) confidence set, the black dashed line at \(0.05\) shows that the set is approximately \([0.25, 0.85]\).

title: Inferential Models
text:
Inferential Models (IMs) were first introduced by the 2015 book, as pictured to the left, by Ryan Martin and Chuanhai Liu.






Inferential Models provide Bayesian style uncertainty quantification, both without the use of a prior, and with Type 1 error control guarantees at any sample size.



We argue that epistemic uncertainty (that a Bayesian posterior captures) is not best captured by probability, but rather through the language of possibility.
This is because






Warning



Any probability distribution over a parameter space will necessarily put arbitrarily high weight on false hypotheses
cite.


We contend that Frequentism and Bayesianism have philosophical flaws, and that the Inferential Model paradigm is one which holds great potential for the future of statistics.
